title: Response to application from respondents Richard Comerford, et al.

pages.text:
Capital Case No. 26A634 
IN THE
SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
JESSE GUARDADO,
Petitioner,
v.
SECRETARY, FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS, ET. AL,
Respondents.
ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE ELEVENTH CIRCUIT
RESPONSE TO APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
EXECUTION SCHEDULED FOR NOVEMBER 5, 2026, AT 6:00 P.M.
On November 3, 2026, Jesse Guardado, represented by Capital Habeas Unit of 
the Office of the Federal Public Defender of the Northern District of Florida 
(CHU─N), filed a petition for a writ of certiorari in this Court in this active warrant 
case. He also filed an application for a stay of the execution for this Court to have 
additional time to decide his pending petition. This Court, however, should simply deny 
the petition for the reasons stated in the brief in opposition and then deny the 
application for a stay of the execution.

2
Stays of Executions
Stays of executions are not granted as “a matter of course.” Hill v. McDonough, 
547 U.S. 573, 583-84 (2006). Rather, a stay is “an equitable remedy” and “equity must 
be sensitive to the State’s strong interest in enforcing its criminal judgments without 
undue interference from the federal courts.” Id. at 584. Both the State and the victims 
of crime have an important interest in the timely enforcement of a sentence. Calderon 
v. Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 556 (1998); Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 149-151
(2019). The people of Florida, as well as surviving victims and their families, “deserve 
better” than the “excessive” delays that now typically occur in capital cases. Bucklew,
587 U.S. at 149.
Moreover, this Court has stated, in the capital context, that “the relative harms
to the parties” must still be considered, including “the State’s significant interest in 
enforcing its criminal judgments.” Nelson v. Campbell, 541 U.S. 637, 649–50 (2004) 
(emphasis added). Without finality, “the criminal law is deprived of much of its 
deterrent effect.” Calderon, 523 U.S. at 555-56. And finality in a capital case is the 
execution. The brutal murder of 75-year-old Jackie Malone occurred over 22 years ago, 
in September of 2004, and Guardado’s convictions and death sentence have been final 
since this Court denied review in 2008. Guardado v. State, 965 So. 2d 108 (Fla. 2007), 
cert. denied, 552 U.S. 1197 (2008) (No. 07–8094).
Guardado’s Eighth Amendment challenge to Florida’s three-drug protocol is sheer 
speculation involving a Goldilocks scenario of getting enough etomidate to remain 
unconscious during the consciousness check but not enough etomidate to remain

3
unconscious a few minutes later when the other two drugs are administered. Guardado 
v. Sec’y, Fla. Dep’t of Corr., No. 26-14027, slip. op. at 9 (11th Cir. Nov. 2, 2026)
(characterizing Guardado’s claim that an insufficient dosage of one drug could lead to 
unnecessary suffering from another drug as “speculation”). This Court has stated that
federal courts, when dealing with “speculative” challenges to a state’s method of 
execution, should “curtail” such § 1983 litigation. Bucklew, 587 U.S. at 151 (stating, in a 
§ 1983 challenge to Missouri’s protocol, that federal courts “can and should protect settled 
state judgments from undue interference by invoking their equitable powers” to “curtail” 
§ 1983 suits “based on speculative theories”); see also Hill, 547 U.S. at 585 (stating that 
“federal courts can and should protect States from dilatory or speculative suits”). 
This Court has also repeatedly stated thatlast minute stays of executions should
be the “extreme exception, not the norm.” Barr v. Lee, 591 U.S. 979, 981 (2020)
(vacating a lower court’s grant of a stay of a federal execution quoting Bucklew, 587 
U.S. at 151). This Court should curtail any further litigation by denying a stay.
The Three Factors Required for a Stay
To be granted a stay of execution in this Court, Guardado must establish three 
factors: (1) a reasonable probability that the Court would vote to grant certiorari; (2) 
a significant possibility of reversal if review was granted; and (3) a likelihood of 
irreparable injury to the applicant in the absence of a stay. Barefoot v. Estelle, 463 U.S. 
880, 895 (1983). He must establish all three Barefoot factors.

4
Probability of this Court granting certiorari
As to the first factor, there is little chance that four justices of this Court would 
vote to grant certiorari review. As explained in detail in the accompanying brief in
opposition, the first question is not worthy of certiorari review.
The federal district court, following an evidentiary hearing, ruled that the 
maladministration challenge to the protocol was meritless based on numerous findings of 
fact, including that the etomidate used in the executions was not expired and the Eleventh 
Circuit concluded that that those factual determinations were not clearly erroneous. 
Guardado v. Sec’y, Fla. Dep’t of Corr., No. 26-14027, slip. op. at 5 (11th Cir. Nov. 2, 2026).
This Court does not typically grant review of questions that are fact bound. See Sup. Ct. 
Rule 10 (stating a petition for a writ of certiorari “is rarely granted when the asserted error 
consists of erroneous factual findings”); United States v. Johnston, 268 U.S. 220, 227 (1925) 
(“We do not grant a certiorari to review evidence and discuss specific facts”); Cash v. 
Maxwell, 565 U.S. 1138 (2012) (statement of Sotomayor, J., respecting the denial of 
certiorari) (stating that a disagreement with a “highly factbound conclusion” is an 
“insufficient basis for granting certiorari.”). This Court would not grant review merely to 
decide whether the district court’s factual findings were clearly erroneous and certainly not 
when the determination that the etomidate was not expired was made, in part, based on 
the judge’s in camera review of additional evidence.
And, as explained in detail in the accompanying brief in opposition, the second 
question is not worthy of certiorari review either. There is a threshold issue regarding state 
confidentiality law. The disclosure of the pharmacy logs risks disclosing the supplier of the

5
drugs.
There is a low probability of this Court granting certiorari review. Guardado 
fails the first Barefoot factor, which alone is sufficient reason to deny his request for 
a stay because he is required to establish all three factors.
Probability of this Court granting relief on the merits
As to the second Barefoot factor, there is little possibility of Guardado prevailing 
on the merits, if this Court were to grant review. 
Guardado would not prevail on the merits of his Eighth Amendment challenge 
to Florida’s protocol. He has not established that there were any deviations from the 
protocol, much less that the deviations presented a “substantial risk” of “serious 
harm” or “severe pain,” as required by this Court’s precedent. Glossip v. Gross, 576 
U.S. 863, 877 (2015). Guardado was granted an evidentiary hearing in the federal 
district court regarding his allegations about the use of expired etomidate, postmortem retrograde extrapolations of etomidate levels, the use of lower doses of the 
other two drugs than the prescribed doses in the protocol, and the use of the 
unauthorized drug of lidocaine, an analgesic. The district court found that the 
etomidate used in the six executions at issue was not expired and, in fact, the correct 
expiration date for that etomidate was 2027.
Nor would Guardado prevail on the issue of whether he should be granted a 
stay of execution to further litigate his § 1983 challenges to Florida’s protocol. The 
equities of a stay are certainly not on his side, after he failed to carry his heavy burden

6
of proof at the evidentiary hearing, especially as to his main allegation regarding the 
use of expired etomidate. This Court has stated that stays “should be the extreme 
exception, not the norm.” Bucklew, 587 U.S. at 150. It would be even more extreme 
to grant an inmate a stay to have a second opportunity to prove a claim after failing 
to do so the first time. 
And he must prevail on the merits of both the Eighth Amendment issue and 
the stay issue in this case because both the district court and the Eleventh Circuit 
denied the stay in large part based on their determinations that the Eighth 
Amendment challenge was meritless.
Guardado would also not prevail on the second question, This Court’s 
precedent holding there is no constitutional right to government information is to the 
contrary.
As explained in detail in the accompanying brief in opposition, Guardado does
not have a “significant” possibility of prevailing in this Court on the merits of either 
question, if this Court were to grant review. Guardado also fails the second Barefoot 
factor.
Irreparable injury
As to the third Barefoot factor of irreparable injury, none is identified in his 
application for a stay. Although the execution will result in his death, that is the 
inherent nature of a death sentence. This Court has repeatedly held that a sentence 
of death is constitutional and has observed that the death penalty was, in fact, “the

7
standard penalty for all serious crimes at the time of the founding.” Bucklew, 587 
U.S. at 129 (stating that the “Constitution allows capital punishment”); Glossip, 576 
U.S. at 867 (noting this Court reaffirmed that the death penalty does not violate the 
Constitution in Gregg v. Georgia, 428 U.S. 153 (1976)). And this Court made those 
observations in the context of § 1983 challenges to states’ lethal-injection protocols. 
The factors for granting a stay are taken from the standard for granting a stay
for normal civil litigation, which is not a natural fit in capital cases. Barefoot, 463 U.S. 
at 895-96 (citing Times-Picayune Pub. Corp. v. Schulingkamp, 419 U.S. 1301, 1305
(1974) (Powell, J., in chambers)). In the capital context, more should be required to
establish irreparable injury than the execution itself, when this Court’s precedent 
clearly establishes that capital punishment is constitutional. Guardado has identified 
no irreparable harm that is not a direct consequence of his valid, constitutional, and
long-final death sentence.
Guardado fails the third Barefoot factor, in addition to failing the other two 
factors.
Accordingly, this Court should deny the application for a stay.
Respectfully submitted,
JAMES UTHMEIER
ATTORNEY GENERAL OF FLORIDA
/s/ Scott A. Browne
